The Sending Church
thuh SEND-ing CHURCH
noun (ecclesiology / missions)
From send, Old English sendan, to cause to go; rendering Greek apostellō. The sending church is the local body that commissions missionaries.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Sending Church is the local congregation that, under Christ's authority, commissions and supports those whom the Spirit calls to the work of the gospel. The pattern is Antioch: "the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away" (Acts 13:2—3). The call originated with the Spirit, but the commissioning was the act of a worshipping local church—fasting, praying, the laying on of hands, the sending. When the work was done, the missionaries returned to Antioch, "from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God for the work which they fulfilled" (Acts 14:26), and "rehearsed all that God had done with them." Thus missionaries are sent men, accountable to the church that sent them, not autonomous agents. This stands against the modern parachurch model that sends apart from any local church's oversight, and against the lone freelancer who answers to none. This dictionary confesses that the Great Commission is given to the church, and that the right ordering of missions is the local congregation, governed by its elders, sending and sustaining the men whom the Lord has called.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The local congregation that, under Christ's authority and through its elders, commissions and supports missionaries; modeled by Antioch in Acts 13, which fasted, prayed, laid on hands, and sent forth Barnabas and Saul.

THE SENDING CHURCH, noun. The local congregation that commissions and supports those called to the gospel work.

Modeled by Antioch, which set apart Barnabas and Saul at the Spirit's word.

It acted by fasting, prayer, the laying on of hands, and the sending away of its men.

It requires that missionaries be sent and held accountable by a local church, and it forbids autonomous, churchless sending.

Its returning men "rehearsed all that God had done," sealing their accountability to the body.

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 13:1 — "Now there were in the church that was at Antioch certain prophets and teachers; as Barnabas, and Simeon that was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, which had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul."

Acts 13:3 — "And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away."

Acts 14:26 — "And thence sailed to Antioch, from whence they had been recommended to the grace of God for the work which they fulfilled."

Acts 14:27 — "And when they were come, and had gathered the church together, they rehearsed all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The modern corruption is the autonomous parachurch and freelance model that sends and supports missionaries apart from the oversight of a local church.

expand to see more

The prevailing corruption is the divorce of missions from the local church. Whole agencies send, support, and govern missionaries with no congregation standing behind them, and many a sincere worker goes out as a lone freelancer accountable to no eldership. The Antioch pattern rebukes this. The Spirit's call came within a worshipping church; the church fasted, prayed, laid on hands, and sent; and the sent men returned to report. Missions is not a private vocation pursued beside the church but a work of the church, extended through her commissioned men.

This is not to deny that believers may cooperate across congregations, for the churches of Macedonia and Achaia joined in the Collection. But cooperation must not displace oversight. The right ordering keeps each missionary anchored in a sending church, governed by elders, sustained and held to account by the body. To recover the Sending Church is to recover the Great Commission as Christ gave it—to His church—and to put an end to the rootless sending that has too often loosed men from the discipline and the prayers of the saints.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Old English sendan, to cause to go, rendering the Greek apostellō, to send forth.

expand to see more

Send is from Old English sendan, to cause to go on a journey or mission.

It renders the Greek apostellō, to send forth with a commission, the root of apostle.

Acts 13:3 uses apelusan, they sent away, after prayer and laying on of hands.

Acts 14:26 uses paradedomenoi, having been committed or recommended to the grace of God.

The terms root missionary sending in the deliberate, ordered act of a local church.

Usage

"Antioch is the model of the Sending Church, fasting and praying before it sent Barnabas and Saul."

"A missionary without a Sending Church to commission and sustain him departs from the Acts pattern."

"The Sending Church holds its missionaries accountable, even as Paul and Barnabas returned to rehearse what God had done."
